about: logicbook14: the "Another way to see it" boxes in the print series and the ebooks (from logic13's $SP/logic13-book-boxes.md, rewritten in the series' natural voice: few colons, at most one "X, not Y" in a box, no stacked punchlines). Each box is one situation from /the-logic-behind-it.html (assets/js/logic-library.js, by its id) in the lens's six parts, tied to one chapter. tools/book/build_series.py prints it before the chapter's "In everyday life" (or "You, in all your relationships", or "Common mix-ups") section, else at the end of the chapter, and ends it with a code (print) or a link (ebook) to /the-logic-behind-it.html?item=<id>#find. refs are research ids on /research.html; they join the chapter's Research notes. No made-up names. The owner's road-rage tip is for the website only and is never used here.

boxes.title: Leaving early without a long goodbye
boxes.looks: Partway through a party, someone slips out with a quick wave.
logic: Energy works like a budget
This evening spent it faster than expected
Staying past empty risks a shutdown or a sharp word
Leaving quietly protects the evening and the friendship
boxes.like: A phone on 3% that switches off everything except the call.
boxes.fits: A long goodbye costs energy too, and there is very little left by then.
boxes.other: The host may wonder what went wrong, or whether you had a bad time.
boxes.say: “I had a good time. When my battery goes, I need to go quickly.”
boxes.step: Send a short thank-you text the next morning.

boxes.title: “I don’t know how I feel”
boxes.looks: Asked how they feel, someone says “I don’t know” and seems stuck.
logic: Feelings start as signals in the body
Some people find those signals hard to read
With no clear signal there is no clear word
So “I don’t know” is the honest answer
boxes.like: A radio caught between two stations.
boxes.fits: Finding feelings hard to name is common, and it is more common among autistic people.
boxes.other: The person asking may feel shut out, or think something is being hidden from them.
boxes.say: “I really don’t know yet. Ask me about my body instead.”
boxes.step: Try simpler questions, such as “More tired or more tense?” and “Space or company?”

boxes.title: Saying sorry all the time
boxes.looks: Someone apologises for asking a question, for being in the way, for taking up room.
logic: An early apology can head off someone else’s anger
The habit was often learned long ago, somewhere it kept things calm
The sorry works like a shield
So it is often about safety more than guilt
boxes.like: Ducking before anything has been thrown.
boxes.fits: The habit made sense where it was learned, even if today is safe.
boxes.other: Constant apologies can sound hollow, or make the listener feel they must have been harsh.
boxes.say: “Sorry is an old habit of mine. I’m learning I don’t need it here.”
boxes.step: Swap one sorry a day for a thank you. “Thanks for waiting” works where “Sorry I’m late” used to.

boxes.title: Wearing headphones at the dinner table
boxes.looks: At a family meal, one person has headphones in.
logic: Sound arrives whether you want it or not
A brain that filters less hears all of it at once
Filtering by hand uses up attention
Headphones do the filtering, so there is attention left for people
boxes.like: Sunglasses on a bright day. You still see everything, without squinting.
boxes.fits: Many people take in more of the background noise. One theory links this to how much the brain smooths out what it hears.
boxes.other: The family may feel shut out of the meal.
boxes.say: “These help me stay at the table.”
boxes.step: Agree a tap on the arm that means “I’m talking to you”, and take one ear out when it comes.

boxes.title: Eating the same lunch every day
boxes.looks: The same sandwich, every day, for years.
logic: Every new food is a small gamble
A known food is a sure thing
Sure things save energy for the rest of the day
So sameness is a way of being efficient
boxes.like: A pilot’s checklist, the same each time on purpose.
boxes.fits: For people with strong senses of taste and texture, a known food takes away an unpleasant surprise.
boxes.other: The cook may feel their food is being turned down.
boxes.say: “It’s safe and easy for me. It says nothing about your cooking.”
boxes.step: Keep one safe option on the table beside anything new.

boxes.title: Snapping when hungry or tired
boxes.looks: A small question at the end of a long day gets a sharp answer.
logic: Patience runs on fuel
Hunger and tiredness drain the tank
With an empty tank, small things feel big
The snap is the fuel gauge talking
boxes.like: A phone on 3% that starts closing apps.
boxes.fits: Poor sleep is linked with more conflict the next day, and hunger can colour our judgements without our noticing.
boxes.other: The person who asked did nothing wrong, and the tone still lands on them.
boxes.say: “I’m running on empty. Can we talk after I’ve eaten?”
boxes.step: Eat first. Then come back and say sorry for the tone.

boxes.title: Getting upset over something “small”
boxes.looks: After a long day, a cup left on the side leads to an outburst.
logic: Stress adds up all day
Each thing fills a glass a little more
The cup is the last drop
What spills is the whole glass
boxes.like: One more breath into a balloon that was already full.
boxes.fits: The last small thing often gets the reaction that belongs to the whole day.
boxes.other: The person who left the cup gets a whole day poured over them.
boxes.say: “It’s not just the cup. It’s been a heavy day.”
boxes.step: Say early when the glass is getting full. Afterwards, apologise for the size of the reaction.

boxes.title: Asking for reassurance again and again
boxes.looks: “Are you sure you’re not angry with me?” for the fourth time tonight.
logic: Doubt feels like danger
Reassurance turns the alarm off for a moment
Then the alarm comes back
Asking again is trying to turn it off again
boxes.like: Going back to check the front door is locked.
boxes.fits: Uncertainty can feel unbearable when you’re anxious, and asking brings real relief, even if it is brief.
boxes.other: Answering again and again is tiring, and it can keep the loop going.
boxes.say: “My worry keeps coming back. Asking turns it down for a bit.”
boxes.step: Agree a kind limit together. One clear answer, then something calming to do side by side.

boxes.title: Fine all day, falling apart at home
boxes.looks: At work or school they’re fine. At home they melt down or go silent.
logic: Fitting in all day takes effort that doesn’t show
The effort is held in until it is safe to stop
Home feels safe, so the holding lets go
The crash shows that home is trusted
boxes.like: Holding your breath underwater and gasping at the surface.
boxes.fits: Autistic adults describe “camouflaging” followed by exhaustion, and many other people do a version of it too.
boxes.other: The family gets the hardest part of the day.
boxes.say: “I hold it together all day. Home is where I can stop.”
boxes.step: A quiet half hour after getting home, with no questions. Later, a line like “That wasn’t about you” helps.

boxes.title: Hinting instead of asking
boxes.looks: “It’s a bit cold in here,” and then annoyance when nobody closes the window.
logic: A direct request can sound like an order
A hint offers the idea without pressure
The other person can take it up as if it were their own idea, or let it pass
Nobody has to give an open no
boxes.like: Leaving a door open for someone, rather than pushing them through it.
boxes.fits: Indirect speech lets people ask while both sides keep face.
boxes.other: Hints get missed, and then both people feel blamed.
boxes.say: “When I hint, I’m trying to be gentle.”
boxes.step: Add the ask to the hint. “It’s cold. Could you close the window?”

boxes.title: Blunt, direct feedback
boxes.looks: “The second half doesn’t work.” No softening at all.
logic: The aim is to help the work be right
Soft words can hide the point
A clear point is quicker to fix
Being direct saves the other person’s time
boxes.like: A sat nav says “Turn left”. It never says “You might consider left.”
boxes.fits: Mix-ups between differently wired people run both ways. The plain speaker isn’t the only one missing signals.
boxes.other: Words land on feelings too, and the listener may feel attacked.
boxes.say: “I’m direct because I trust you with the real answer.”
boxes.step: Start with one warm line, then give the fact.

boxes.title: Small talk about the weather
boxes.looks: Two near-strangers spend five minutes on the weather.
logic: Strangers need a safe way to check each other out
The weather carries no risk
Easy lines say “I’m friendly, you can relax”
Once both feel safe, real talk can start
boxes.like: Musicians tuning up before the concert.
boxes.fits: Brief, friendly chats with people we hardly know are linked with feeling more connected that day.
boxes.other: For people who find it pointless, it costs energy and gives no information.
boxes.say: “Small talk is how I say hello.”
boxes.step: Keep two easy lines and one real question ready, then steer towards something you care about.

boxes.title: Going quiet in an argument
boxes.looks: Mid-row, one person stops answering and stares at the floor.
logic: A fast argument floods the body
A flooded brain struggles to find good words
Silence stops the bad words getting out
Going quiet is a way of braking
boxes.like: Pulling over in heavy rain until you can see the road.
boxes.fits: Arguments that turn more negative than positive go with more trouble later, and a pause can stop that slide.
boxes.other: For someone who needs to settle things, silence can feel like being left.
boxes.say: “I’m going quiet so I don’t say something I don’t mean.”
boxes.step: Always name a time to come back, and then come back at that time.

boxes.title: Showing love by doing more than saying
boxes.looks: One partner rarely says “I love you”, but fixes the bike and makes the lunches.
logic: Love can be said or done
For some people, doing feels truer than saying
Fixing the bike is the message
The words are in the action
boxes.like: Two languages for the same sentence.
boxes.fits: People show care in different ways, and practical help can be the clearest way some people have.
boxes.other: A partner who hears love in words may feel unloved, even surrounded by kind acts.
boxes.say: “Fixing your bike was me saying I love you.”
boxes.step: One word and one deed each. Say it on the way out, and notice the deeds out loud.

boxes.title: Doing everything at the last minute
boxes.looks: The form had a month. It gets done the night before.
logic: Interest and urgency switch the engine on
A far-off deadline doesn’t
The deadline arriving finally does
So late work is more a starting problem than a caring problem
boxes.like: A car that only starts when you roll it down a hill.
boxes.fits: For many people with ADHD, starting depends on urgency more than on importance.
boxes.other: The other person carries the worry of not knowing, which is invisible work too.
boxes.say: “I care about this. My brain starts late.”
boxes.step: Set an earlier, shared check-in date the other person can count on.

boxes.title: Redoing a job someone else already did
boxes.looks: One person loads the dishwasher. The other quietly reloads it.
logic: Things have a system for a reason
Something in the “wrong” place means hunting for it later
Putting it back saves hassle tomorrow
So it is about the system more than the effort
boxes.fits: People who rely on a system feel the cost of a broken one more strongly.
boxes.other: The person who did the job feels criticised, and may stop helping.
boxes.say: “Thank you for doing it. I moved a few things for my own system, and you didn’t do it badly.”
boxes.step: Agree which jobs need a set way, write it down, and say thanks first.

boxes.title: Cancelling plans after a long week
boxes.looks: Friday afternoon. “So sorry, I can’t make tonight.”
logic: Energy comes back with rest
This week spent all of it
Going out on empty means being there in body only
Cancelling spares everyone a flat, tired evening
boxes.like: Not driving when you’re too tired to drive safely.
boxes.fits: A full stress tank changes what anyone has to give.
boxes.other: The friend may have cleared their evening and been looking forward to it.
boxes.say: “I’m empty, not uninterested. Can we pick a new day now?”
boxes.step: Cancel early, offer a new date in the same message, and plan lighter evenings when the weeks run full.

boxes.title: Different ideas of “on time”
boxes.looks: One person is ready at seven sharp. The other thinks seven means “from seven”.
logic: “Seven o’clock” is read through a rule learned at home
In some families it means exactly seven, in others roughly seven
Each person turns up when their own rule says is polite
Neither is careless. They read the same words differently
boxes.fits: Families, workplaces and kinds of event all keep time differently.
boxes.other: Whoever waits may feel unimportant, and the dinner goes cold.
boxes.say: “Where I grew up, seven meant from seven.”
boxes.step: Say which kind of time you mean. “Seven sharp, the table’s booked.”

boxes.title: Needing it in writing
boxes.looks: After a chat about who does what, someone asks, “Could you write that down?”
logic: Spoken words vanish as they’re said
Holding them in mind while doing the job splits attention
Written steps can be checked again
Asking for writing means wanting to get it right
boxes.like: A recipe card, rather than a cook calling instructions from the next room.
boxes.fits: Working memory differs a lot between people, and writing turns memory into something you can rely on.
boxes.other: It can sound like distrust of what was agreed.
boxes.say: “I ask for it in writing so I get it right. I trust what we agreed.”
boxes.step: End each look-back with a two-line written summary.
